paragraphs.heading: What flips
paragraphs.text: A geomagnetic reversal is a swap in Earth's magnetic field in which magnetic north and magnetic south trade places. This concerns the magnetic poles, not the geographic North and South Poles. Over time the field has switched between normal polarity, pointing the way it does today, and reverse polarity, pointing the opposite way. Each of these stretches is called a chron. The flips seem to come at random, with at least 183 in the past 83 million years, or about one every 450,000 years on average.

paragraphs.heading: How long a flip takes
paragraphs.text: The most recent, the Brunhes–Matuyama reversal, happened 780,000 years ago, and estimates of how fast it went vary widely. Some sources put the four latest reversals at about 7,000 years each on average; others give a range of 2,000 to 12,000 years, with some possibly lasting as long as 70,000. Shorter events, in which the field turned over for only a few hundred years, are called excursions rather than full reversals; the Laschamp excursion is one. During an excursion, only the liquid outer core flips its field, while the solid inner core does not.

paragraphs.heading: Early clues in lava
paragraphs.text: In the early 1900s, geologists including Bernard Brunhes found volcanic rocks magnetized opposite to the local field. In the late 1920s Motonori Matuyama gathered the first systematic evidence, noticing that every rock with a reversed field was from the early Pleistocene or older. Few people took much interest at the time, since Earth's polarity was poorly understood. Later work showed that most magnetized volcanic rocks keep a trace of the field as it was when they cooled through a point called the Curie temperature.

paragraphs.heading: Putting dates on the flips
paragraphs.text: Without reliable ways to find a rock's age, scientists at first thought reversals came roughly every million years. Better radiometric dating in the 1950s changed that. At the United States Geological Survey, Allan Cox and Richard Doell, joined by geochronologist Brent Dalrymple, set out to learn whether flips came at regular intervals, and in 1959 they produced the first magnetic-polarity time scale. A team led by Neil Opdyke found the same pattern of flips in sediments from deep-sea cores.

paragraphs.heading: Stripes on the sea floor
paragraphs.text: In the 1950s and 1960s, research ships gathered magnetic readings, but only when the data were plotted on maps did regular, continuous magnetic stripes appear across the ocean floors. In 1963 Frederick Vine and Drummond Matthews explained them: new sea floor rock takes on the direction of the field as it forms. If the floor spreads out from a central ridge, it builds pairs of stripes running parallel to that ridge. This idea was the first key test of seafloor spreading.

paragraphs.heading: Reading older rocks
paragraphs.text: No sea floor still in place is older than about 180 million years, so earlier flips must be found another way. Most sedimentary rocks hold tiny amounts of iron-rich minerals that line up with the field when they form, and they keep that record unless later chemical, physical or biological change wipes it out. The current time scale lists 184 polarity intervals in the last 83 million years. The pace of flips has varied a lot: around 72 million years ago, the field reversed five times within a million years.
